pos.personaBrief: The Scheiberlspiel of 'schnelle, kurze, trickreiche Kombinationen' and Sindelar's 1929 call to 'noch mehr scheiberln' put keeping and circulating the ball at the core; the 1932 English press praised the Kombinationsgabe, even though the team 'regularly lacked efficiency'.

pro.personaBrief: Short flat passes and Hogan's 'constructive football with every pass... an object' favour building up through combinations over quick direct attacks, but the attacking centre-half Smistik was known for line-breaking long balls from the back, so progression was not purely lateral.

est.personaBrief: The 'Danubian Whirl' meant 'the interchanging of the five forward players' with 'such fluidity' (Viennese whirlpool), and a slightly deep-lying centre forward (Sindelar as playmaker) combining in tight short-passing triangles: a relational structure inside a nominal 2-3-5.

lar.personaBrief: The 2-3-5 always fielded two wingers (Zischek, Vogl), but critics noted an 'unwillingness to dribble' and the play ran through the combinations of Sindelar, the inside forwards and the attacking centre-half, so the route to goal was mainly central with wingers as part of the interchange.

blo.personaBrief: No verified evidence on pressing or block height (gap axis); from general knowledge, inter-war 2-3-5 teams did not press collectively, forwards saved themselves for attacking, and the only (unverified) hint is the defence retreating at Stamford Bridge 1932, consistent with an attack-first side that regrouped rather than hunted the ball.

mar.personaBrief: No verified evidence on marking (gap axis); from general knowledge, the pre-WM 2-3-5 with two backs covering the centre and half-backs picking up wingers was essentially positional/zonal, and the tight man-marking in 1934 was Italy's plan against Austria, not Austria's own.

pla.personaBrief: Meisl's half-time cry 'Spüts euer Spüü!' at Stamford Bridge and Austria concentrating on 'their waltz' while Italy prepared a physical game in 1934 show a school that played its own way whatever the opponent.

res.personaBrief: Called 'Viennese football art' (Tschammer, 1938) and remembered for the 4-3 defeat in London as much as for wins, the style valued beauty even while it 'regularly lacked efficiency'; no explicit Meisl or Hogan statement, so this leans on reputation.

sis.personaBrief: The game was a collective combination system, and critics regretted the lack of 'individual effort' and dribbling, yet its centre was Sindelar's freedom as the 'Mozart of football' playmaker who 'had brains in his legs', so it mixes collective passing with licence for the star.

jog.personaBrief: The 'sophisticated, advanced and technical approach of the Austrians' against 'robust, physically strong Germans', the slight technician Sindelar as star and Smistik's passing from centre-half make technique clearly the priority over physique.

bas.personaBrief: The Wunderteam was kept together until 'most were the wrong side of 30' at the 1934 World Cup, favouring an established core over renewal, though Hiden did replace the more experienced Franzl in 1931.

lid.personaBrief: Goldblatt calls Meisl 'disciplinarian' and Sindelar fell out of his favour for years; the 1931 recall came from journalists at the Ring-Café, not from players, so authority sat with the Teamchef.
